rows.label: Formula
rows.text:
$$\Delta x\,\Delta p\ge\frac{h}{4\pi}$$ (forbids definite orbits)
$$Z_{\text{eff}}=Z-S$$ (screening, ignored by Bohr's model — cause of failure for multi-electron atoms)
En(H) = −13.6 Z²/n² eV

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: ❌ Bohr's theory is completely wrong and useless. ✅ It is quantitatively excellent for one-electron species (H, He⁺) and is still used there; the defects appear beyond that scope.  ·  ❌ Fine structure arises because of many electrons. ✅ It arises from relativistic effects and electron spin even in a one-electron atom.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: Sommerfeld (1916) added elliptical orbits and the azimuthal quantum number to explain fine structure.  ·  Schrödinger's wave equation (1926) replaced orbits with orbitals and remains the working theory of the atom.

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: **Problem:** Why is the ground-state radius of He⁺ half that of hydrogen? **Solution:** r₁ = 0.529 n²/Z Å = 0.529/2 = 0.2645 Å — the formula works because He⁺ has one electron, and fails for neutral helium.  ·  **Problem:** Show a Bohr orbit violates the uncertainty principle for H (n = 1). **Solution:** a fixed r gives Δx ≈ 0 and a definite speed gives Δp ≈ 0, so Δx·Δp → 0 < h/4π — impossible; hence the orbit is not a real trajectory.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: Covers only: defects of bohr's theory (within Atomic Structure).  ·  Out of scope here: topics of neighbouring units in Chemistry — don't mix them.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: ### 1. Meaning  ·  Bohr's model is **semi-classical**: it keeps classical circular orbits and Coulomb mechanics but bolts on an unexplained quantum condition (mvr = nh/2π). Its defects are exactly where classical thinking and the single-electron assumption break down.

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: Sodium D lines (589.0 and 589.6 nm) are the standard example of fine structure unexplained by Bohr's model.  ·  Bohr model: electron in fixed circular orbits; angular momentum mvr = nh/2π; energy En = −13.6 eV·Z²/n² (for H, Z=1).

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: state + explain the main idea of "Defects of Bohr's theory" with one example.  ·  compare "Defects of Bohr's theory" with the related idea from a neighbouring unit.

rows.label: Hints
rows.text: Answer in this order: one-electron only → fine structure → Zeeman/Stark → intensities → uncertainty principle → wave–particle duality → ad hoc postulates.  ·  Do not mix 'defects of Bohr's theory' with 'limitations of Rutherford's model' — marks are lost by quoting the wrong list.

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: • Defects of Bohr's theory

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: Rydberg/Balmer series: 1/λ = R(H)(1/n₁² − 1/n₂²). Absorption/emission = ΔE = hν between levels.  ·  Four quantum numbers: n (shell), l (subshell, 0…n−1), mₗ (orientation, −l…+l), mₛ (spin ±½). Orbitals: s (spherical), p (dumbbell).

rows.label: More practice
rows.text: solve / apply for "Defects of Bohr's theory" and verify the answer is plausible.

rows.label: Extra solved
rows.text: Worked: identify given → pick sub-concept → apply standard form → check units / edges.  ·  **Problem:** Where does the Bohr–Bury scheme first fail? **Solution:** at potassium (Z = 19): the 2n²/sequence rules put the 19th electron in the M shell, but experiment and the (n + l) rule place it in 4s — the first sign that subshell energies, not shells, control filling.

rows.label: MCQ drill
rows.text: A common examiner point on "Defects of Bohr's theory" is that a statement is only valid when its condition of applicability is met. Is that TRUE or FALSE? → True  ·  According to the Bohr–Bury scheme, the maximum electrons in the outermost shell is: → B

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: ### 2. Works only for one-electron species  ·  It succeeds for H, He⁺, Li²⁺, Be³⁺ but fails for He, Li and every multi-electron atom: electron–electron repulsion and the screening (shielding) of nuclear charge by inner electrons are ignored, so calculated energies do not match experiment.  ·  ### 3. Cannot explain fine structure (line splitting)

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: hν = ΔE  ·  λ = h/(mv) (de Broglie)  ·  $$\text{shell capacity}=2n^{2}:\ K\ 2,\ L\ 8,\ M\ 18,\ N\ 32;\qquad \text{valence shell}\le 8$$

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: $$\Delta x\,\Delta p\ge\frac{h}{4\pi}\ (\text{forbids definite orbits});\qquad Z_{\text{eff}}=Z-S\ (\text{screening, absent from Bohr})$$  ·  $$n\lambda=2\pi r\ \text{with }\lambda=\frac{h}{mv}\ \Rightarrow\ mvr=\frac{nh}{2\pi}$$  ·  $$\lambda=\frac{h}{mv}=\frac{3.32\times10^{-10}\ \text{m for }n=1\ (\text{H})}{}$$

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: ❌ The uncertainty principle reflects imperfect instruments. ✅ It is a fundamental limit of nature, not a measurement limitation.  ·  ❌ Bohr failed because orbits are not circular. ✅ The fatal objection is that a definite orbit (simultaneous r and p) cannot exist; probability orbitals replace them.  ·  ❌ Zeeman splitting is explained by Bohr's model. ✅ It requires the magnetic quantum number and orbital magnetic moment of the quantum-mechanical model.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: ❌ skip the key fact → ✅ bohr model: electron in fixed circular orbits; angular momentum mvr = nh/2π; energy en = −13.6 ev·z²/n² (for h, z=1)..  ·  ❌ The M shell can hold 18 electrons before the N shell starts. ✅ The outermost shell is capped at 8; after 8 electrons in M, filling of N begins.  ·  ❌ The Bohr–Bury scheme is a quantum-mechanical theory. ✅ It is a shell-filling rule set from the Bohr orbit picture; subshells and orbital shapes are absent.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: ❌ 2n² applies to the outermost shell. ✅ 2n² is the *capacity*; the octet rule (8) restricts the valence shell's occupancy.  ·  ❌ Bohr's theory failed completely. ✅ It is exact for one-electron species (H, He⁺) — defects appear only beyond that scope.  ·  ❌ Fine structure needs many electrons. ✅ It comes from spin and relativity even in hydrogen.
